summary:
We developed Água Molhada Mission Lab, an educational game that helps people learn about space exploration by designing and testing missions. Players choose destinations, scientific objectives, and equipment while balancing budget, mass, power, fuel, and communication.
The project addresses the challenge of planning space missions by showing how these choices depend on one another. A 3D simulation illustrates launch, orbit, and the journey to the destination, while a report explains why the mission achieved its objective or failed and suggests improvements. Historical rainfall and temperature data from NASA POWER also connect lessons about space with the study of Earth.
With three difficulty levels and individual or team activities, we aim to make complex concepts more accessible. The project turns trial and error into learning, encouraging scientific thinking, collaboration, and interest in space engineering.
details:
Água Molhada Mission Lab is a browser-based educational game that introduces space mission design through experimentation. Players choose from 12 destinations, define a scientific objective, and select instruments, spacecraft systems, a launcher, and an orbit. They must balance budget, mass, power, fuel, communications, and mission duration. Three difficulty levels and interfaces in English and Portuguese make the experience approachable for learners with different backgrounds.

The game connects planning decisions to visible consequences. A 3D simulation presents launch, Earth orbit, travel, and arrival at the destination. Before scientific operations begin, players choose how frequently to collect observations and how to transmit their data. These choices affect resource use and the mission’s outcome. The final report explains success or failure with numerical evidence, identifies the first critical problem, and suggests recalculated improvements. Players can revise their designs, compare saved versions, and export PDF reports.

Our creative approach combines mission planning, visual storytelling, and feedback in one learning cycle. Failure becomes an opportunity to understand a decision and improve it. Contextual explanations, quizzes, and checklists support this process. Teams of two to four participants can divide responsibilities, discuss compromises, and review a shared design using the same screen or exchanged project configurations.

NASA information provides scientific context. Historical rainfall and temperature data from NASA POWER/MERRA-2 connect space-related learning with Earth science. These records are presented separately from the game’s educational engineering calculations. NASA educational references also informed explanations of propulsion and orbital motion. The simulation uses simplified models and compressed visual scales and time to support learning; it does not predict the performance of real spacecraft.

We developed the application using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, with Three.js and WebGL for the interactive 3D environment and jsPDF for downloadable reports. Browser local storage saves designs, while JSON files and configuration links support sharing. Node.js supports automated testing, and Python supports development and packaging tasks. Netlify hosts the website’s files in the cloud, while the game runs in the user’s browser. No specialized hardware is required beyond a computer with a compatible browser. OpenAI Codex assisted with development and design.

Throughout development, our team considered scientific objectives, instrument compatibility, launch capacity, orbital coverage, environmental protection, and the competing demands on limited resources. We also considered clarity, browser performance, different experience levels, and collaboration. Our intended impact is to bring mission planning into classrooms and other learning environments, helping students practice scientific reasoning, discuss engineering choices, and explore their interest in space through accessible, hands-on experimentation.
